Fyodor Dostoevsky. A Russian novelist who excavated the depths of human conscience and psychological torment with unprecedented intensity. Imprisoned for political conspiracy as a young man, he channeled suffering into fiction exploring guilt, faith, doubt, and moral transgression. His major novels—Crime and Punishment, The Brothers Karamazov, The Idiot, and Notes from Underground—are interrogations of the self under extreme philosophical stress, and they redefined what fiction could achieve in penetrating consciousness. Born in Moscow in eighteen twenty-one to a military-physician family, he showed early literary talent but turned to radical politics in the eighteen forties, joining discussion circles critical of Tsarism. Arrested in eighteen forty-nine for involvement in a radical group, he was sentenced to death, reprieved at the scaffold in a psychological terror orchestrated by the Tsar, then exiled to Siberia for four years of hard labor. Prison transformed his worldview; he abandoned radicalism and returned to Russian Orthodoxy, though haunted by doubt. Prison became the forge of his greatest art. He suffered lifelong epilepsy, possibly triggered by trauma, along with financial instability and addiction to gambling; these struggles directly inform his fiction's depiction of human fragmentation. Notes from Underground, published in eighteen sixty-four, is a short, bitter novella of a clerk's inner rage and moral paralysis; it is a proto-existentialist exploration of consciousness itself. Crime and Punishment, published in eighteen sixty-six, features Raskolnikov, an impoverished student who murders a pawnbroker to test his theory that extraordinary men transcend morality. Pursued by detective Porfiry Petrovich, he spirals into guilt and confession. The Idiot, published in eighteen sixty-nine, features Prince Myshkin, a holy fool of saintly innocence, who moves through St. Petersburg society and proves unable to bridge the gap between Christian virtue and human corruption. Demons, also known as The Possessed, published in eighteen seventy-two, is a political thriller about radical nihilists infiltrating a provincial town; it is a dark prophecy about revolutionary violence and moral emptiness. The Brothers Karamazov, published between eighteen seventy-nine and eighteen eighty, is his masterpiece. Four brothers—Dmitri, Ivan, Alyosha, and Smerdyakov—struggle with faith, desire, and murder after their father's death. Ivan's Grand Inquisitor chapter is perhaps the greatest sustained meditation on faith and doubt in literature. Dostoevsky was an inventor of the psychological novel: interior monologue, stream of thought, and extreme introspection serve as the primary action, with plot happening inside characters' minds. He was obsessed with extremes: the nihilist who murders to prove a theory, the saint who cannot exist in the world, the believer torn by doubt—always pushing characters to breaking points. His novels are constituted of arguments, confessions, and disputations where characters articulate ideologies that collide. Russian Orthodox faith and European rational doubt remain in constant tension; no easy resolutions emerge. His novels ask whether suffering and evil can be rationalized or only endured and forgiven. Dostoevsky reinvented the novel as an instrument for philosophical and psychological exploration. Crime and Punishment became the template for psychological thrillers; The Brothers Karamazov is considered by many the greatest novel ever written. His influence spreads far beyond literature to psychoanalysis, existentialist philosophy, and twentieth-century writers from Kafka to Camus to Bellow.
